glyph_origin: 漢: semantic 水 (“water”) + phonetic 熯. Earliest attested in early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, e.g. the 京師畯尊 (銘圖 11784), where it is used as a river name: 王涉漢伐楚. 熯 (⿱𦰩火) depicts a person bound behind the back, mouth open toward the sky, over fire. It may be related to 灘, 歎, 嘆, 熯, 暵, and 難, in senses connected with drought, burning, or exclamation. From the middle Western Zhou onward, 𦰩 may have been confused with 黃. The use as a name for the Chinese ethnicity is generally dated to the Northern Dynasties. It was promoted by the Tuoba-Xianbei-led Northern Wei as a political exonym to deny the legitimacy of the Eastern Jin court and dissolve the residual 晉人 (Jin People) identity in the former Western Jin lands, while appealing to the prestige of the Han dynasty. The appellation was initially resisted as pejorative and was still avoided in the early Tang, only gradually becoming widely accepted as an ethnic name from the mid-to-late Tang onward. Prior to this period, the Chinese referred mostly their land as 華夏 and referred themselves as 諸華/諸夏, and from the Qin dynasty onwards as 華人 or simply as subjects of the ruling dynasty (e.g. 秦人, 漢人, 魏人, 晉人, 宋人, 齊人...)
s_page_origin: Simplified from 漢 (elimination of right component to 又) in the 1956 Chinese Character Simplification Scheme by the People's Republic of China. Not known to have existed prior to that.
senses: [hàn] Han River, a major tributary of the Yangtze River
[hàn] (literary) the Milky Way; by extension, the sky; the heavens
note: glyph_origin is from the traditional page 漢; s_page_origin explains the simplified 汉.
